promptText: What structurally distinguishes a sequence modeling problem from a standard supervised learning problem over tabular features?
options: The model's output must be sensitive to the order of and relationships between input elements, not just their individual values
Sequence models require a strictly larger training dataset than tabular models
Sequence models can only be trained with unsupervised objectives
Sequence models always need GPU hardware, while tabular models fit on a CPU
explanation: A feedforward/tabular model treats its input as an order-independent set of features; a genuine sequence model must be sensitive to permutation, since reordering elements can (and often should) change the output.

promptText: An n-gram language model assumes the probability of the next token depends only on a fixed number of preceding tokens. What is the direct structural consequence of this assumption?
options: It is a truncated approximation of the exact chain-rule factorization, discarding any information beyond the fixed window no matter how relevant
It becomes bidirectional, since it can no longer distinguish past from future tokens
It requires backpropagation through time to train, unlike a Transformer
It automatically resolves out-of-vocabulary words via subword merging
explanation: The chain rule factorization is exact for any history length; the n-gram's Markov assumption approximates each conditional using only the last n-1 tokens, which is precisely why it hits a fixed-window ceiling regardless of how relevant older context is.

promptText: The chain rule of probability lets P(x1, ..., xT) be rewritten as the product of P(xt | x1, ..., x_{t-1}) over all t. Why is this decomposition considered exact rather than an approximation?
options: It follows directly from the mathematical definition of conditional probability and holds for any joint distribution over any sequence whatsoever
It only holds when the sequence satisfies the Markov property
It is exact only for sequences produced by an RNN or Transformer, not for natural language
It is an empirical approximation whose accuracy is validated by measuring perplexity
explanation: The factorization is an identity by definition of conditional probability; what differs between n-grams, RNNs, and Transformers is purely how each conditional term is estimated, not whether the factorization itself holds.

promptText: Why can't a bidirectional RNN be used directly to generate text token by token?
options: Its backward pass requires the entire sequence to already exist, but during generation the future tokens don't exist yet
Bidirectional RNNs are structurally incompatible with gating mechanisms like LSTM or GRU cells
Bidirectional RNNs are simply too slow at inference to ever generate one token at a time
Bidirectional RNNs lack any hidden state that could be carried forward across timesteps
explanation: A bidirectional RNN's right-to-left pass needs the full sequence up front; generation produces the sequence incrementally, so there is nothing for a backward pass to run over — this is a structural limitation, not a training or speed issue.

promptText: On a model evaluation report, Model A shows a lower perplexity than Model B on the same held-out text. What does this indicate?
options: Model A assigns higher average probability to the actual next tokens in the held-out data, i.e. it is less 'surprised' by real text
Model A has fewer trainable parameters than Model B
Model A was trained with teacher forcing while Model B was not
Model A was evaluated on longer sequences than Model B
explanation: Perplexity is the exponentiated average cross-entropy loss; a lower value means the model's predicted probability for the true next token was higher on average, which is a direct measure of predictive fit, not of model size or training procedure.

promptText: Why do Transformers use layer normalization instead of batch normalization?
options: Layer norm normalizes across the feature dimension per token independently, avoiding batch-statistics contamination from padding and the training/inference batch-size mismatch that batch norm suffers from
Layer norm requires strictly fewer learned parameters than batch normalization
Batch normalization cannot mathematically be computed on GPU hardware
Layer norm removes the need for residual connections around each sublayer
explanation: Batch norm computes statistics across the batch dimension, which is awkward with variable-length padded sequences and behaves differently at large-batch training time versus batch-size-1 inference; layer norm's per-token, per-feature normalization has no such dependency.

promptText: A sequence model trained with teacher forcing shows excellent training-time metrics, but its generated outputs drift further off track after an early mistake during actual use. What explains this gap?
options: Exposure bias: training conditions on the true previous token at every step, but inference must condition on the model's own possibly-imperfect generated history, so early errors push the model onto an increasingly off-distribution context
The model overfit the training set and simply needs stronger regularization
Teacher forcing disables gradient clipping, so gradients explode once generation begins
The training loss function does not match the model's architecture
explanation: Teacher forcing makes training stable and parallelizable precisely because it hides this mismatch; at inference there is no ground truth to feed back in, so compounding self-generated errors (exposure bias) are a real production behavior that training metrics never surface.

promptText: Why does a random, row-shuffled train/test split on time-series or conversational data typically produce inflated evaluation metrics?
options: It violates the i.i.d. assumption the split relies on — correlated neighboring timesteps leak information between train and test sets
Random splitting always shrinks the training set below a usable minimum size
It forces the evaluation pipeline to use bidirectional processing even for causal tasks
It changes the vocabulary distribution between the train and test partitions
explanation: Sequential data is correlated by construction, so a random split lets information from timesteps adjacent to (or after) a test point leak into training through correlated neighbors; the correct approach is a strict chronological split.

promptText: Comparing the three general strategies for how much of the past a sequence model can use, which statement correctly captures the trade-off?
options: Compressed running state (e.g., an RNN's hidden state) uses constant memory per step but loses fidelity to distant history through repeated compression, while direct full-history access (attention) preserves fidelity at the cost of compute and memory that scale with sequence length
Fixed-window models like n-grams have effectively unlimited memory of history but are the most computationally expensive of the three
Attention-based models compress the entire history into one fixed-size summary vector, the same way HMMs do
All three strategies have identical computational cost and differ only in how they are implemented in code
explanation: The chapter's central taxonomy is a cost-vs-fidelity trade-off: fixed windows are cheap but structurally blind beyond their edge, compressed state is cheap per step but decays over distance, and full-history attention is the most faithful but scales cost with sequence length.

promptText: In an RNN trained with backpropagation through time, why does gradient signal from many timesteps in the past tend to vanish before it reaches the earliest weights?
options: The gradient involves a product of many Jacobians of the recurrence, and when the dominant eigenvalue of that Jacobian is below 1 (typical with tanh/sigmoid activations), the product shrinks geometrically with the number of steps
The optimizer's learning rate automatically decays toward zero as more timesteps are processed
Weight sharing across timesteps means only the most recent timestep ever contributes a nonzero gradient
Cross-entropy loss becomes mathematically undefined beyond a fixed number of timesteps
explanation: BPTT's gradient for a state k steps back is roughly k repeated multiplications by the recurrence Jacobian; with tanh/sigmoid derivatives bounded well under 1, that product decays exponentially with k, starving early weights of long-range training signal.

promptText: Compared to an LSTM, why does a GRU typically have fewer parameters per layer, and what practical trade-off follows from this?
options: A GRU merges the cell state and hidden state and uses only three weight matrices (reset, update, candidate) versus the LSTM's four, making it cheaper and often faster to train, though the LSTM's extra output gate and separate cell state can still edge it out on more complex long-range tasks
A GRU removes gating entirely and relies on the same plain multiplicative update as a vanilla RNN
A GRU can only process sequences in one direction, whereas an LSTM is inherently bidirectional
A GRU replaces all gates with a single attention mechanism, eliminating the need for learned weight matrices
explanation: An LSTM has four gate/candidate weight matrices while a GRU has three, giving the GRU roughly 75% of an equivalently-sized LSTM's parameters; this makes GRUs attractive under compute or data constraints, while LSTMs' extra capacity can help on harder long-range tasks.

promptText: In scaled dot-product attention, what specifically goes wrong if the sqrt(d_k) scaling term is omitted?
options: Raw dot-product scores grow in magnitude as dimensionality increases, pushing the softmax toward a near one-hot distribution whose gradient is close to zero, which can stall learning of the attention weights
The Query and Key matrices would be forced to have identical shapes, breaking multi-head attention entirely
The attention output would no longer sum to a valid probability distribution over positions
Positional encodings would be applied twice to every token embedding
explanation: Dot-product variance grows linearly with d_k, so unscaled scores get large purely as a side effect of dimensionality; feeding that into softmax saturates it into an overconfident, poorly-gradiented distribution, which the sqrt(d_k) division corrects.

promptText: A candidate claims LSTMs 'solve' the vanishing gradient problem. What is the more precise correction, and under what condition does the LSTM's fix actually break down?
options: LSTMs make the cell-state update additive (c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ ĉ_t), so gradients flow largely undiminished when the forget gate stays near 1 — but gradient flow still degrades if the forget gate saturates near 0 or the model correctly learns to forget aggressively for the task
LSTMs eliminate vanishing gradients entirely by replacing all matrix multiplications with attention, with no remaining failure mode at any sequence length
LSTMs only prevent vanishing gradients during inference; the problem persists identically during training
LSTMs solve vanishing gradients by removing the tanh activation from the recurrence, leaving a purely linear update
explanation: The additive cell-state update creates a near-identity gradient path when the forget gate is close to 1, forming a 'gradient superhighway,' but this only holds conditionally — aggressive forgetting or gate saturation still degrades long-range gradient flow, which is why LSTMs extend usable dependency length rather than removing the ceiling altogether.

promptText: Naive beam search, scored by summed log-probabilities, tends to favor shorter output sequences. Why does this happen mechanically, and how is it corrected?
options: Every additional token contributes a zero-or-negative log-probability term, so shorter sequences accumulate fewer negative terms and score higher by default; length normalization divides the summed log-probability by sequence length to correct for this bias
Shorter sequences are favored because beam search always terminates at the very first end-of-sequence token it encounters, regardless of score, and the fix is to widen the beam
Longer sequences trigger the causal mask to silently block valid attention positions, lowering their score, and the fix is to remove causal masking at inference time
Beam search favors shorter sequences because softmax temperature increases automatically with sequence length, and the fix is to lower the temperature
explanation: Since sequence scores are sums of negative log-probabilities, more tokens mechanically means a more negative (lower) total score under naive summation; dividing by length (or a length exponent) rescales the comparison to per-token quality rather than penalizing completeness.

promptText: Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose tokens that a large target model verifies in parallel. Why can this speed up generation while producing output provably identical in distribution to standard target-model-only decoding?
options: Each draft token is accepted with probability equal to the ratio of the target model's probability to the draft model's probability (capped at 1), and any rejected token is replaced by a corrected sample from the target distribution — a rejection-sampling scheme constructed so the accepted output's marginal distribution exactly matches the target model's own step-by-step generation
The draft and target models' output distributions are averaged together, which approximates the target model closely enough in practice to be treated as identical
The speedup comes from skipping the softmax computation for draft tokens entirely, introducing a small but acceptable bias into the output distribution
Scoring a fixed sequence in parallel is mathematically equivalent to greedy decoding, so the target model's output becomes deterministic and matches by definition
explanation: The acceptance/rejection rule is a formal rejection-sampling argument, not an approximation: it guarantees the final accepted token's distribution is exactly what the target model would have produced alone, so the speedup comes purely from parallelizing verification, never from changing what gets generated.
